title: Traditional Sorghum Beers of Africa | Craft Beer School
desc: Umqombothi, pito, dolo and tella: how traditional African sorghum beers are made, why they are opaque and how they taste.
teaser: Thick, tart and alive in the pot. Africa's sorghum beers are some of the oldest brewing traditions still going.
standfirst: Across much of Africa, beer has been brewed from sorghum for a very long time. These beers are cloudy, sour, low in alcohol and drunk while still fermenting. Here is how they are made, what the main traditions are and why they matter to brewers anywhere.
sections:
Sorghum was domesticated in Africa and thrives where barley struggles: hot, dry land with unreliable rain. That made it the natural brewing grain across large parts of the continent. Millet plays a similar role in some regions. Maize has joined the mix since it arrived from the Americas.

Indian readers know sorghum as jowar, grown widely across the Deccan for rotis and fodder. The same tough grain that feeds people in Maharashtra and Karnataka has been malted and brewed into beer in Africa for generations.

Each region has its own version. Umqombothi is the traditional beer of the Xhosa and other communities in South Africa, made from sorghum malt and maize. Pito is brewed in northern Ghana and Nigeria. Dolo is common in Burkina Faso and Mali. Burukutu is another Nigerian sorghum beer. In Ethiopia, tella is brewed from grains such as teff, barley or sorghum, often with leaves of the gesho plant for bitterness.

Methods vary, but most share a pattern. Sorghum is malted, cooked, soured and fermented. The beer is drunk within days, often straight from the pot, at family and community gatherings.
How sorghum is malted and mashed

Malting sorghum works like malting barley. The grain is steeped, allowed to sprout for several days and then dried in the sun. Sprouting develops enzymes that can convert starch into sugar, though sorghum malt is generally weaker in some of those enzymes than barley malt.

Sorghum starch also needs more heat to soften than barley starch, with gelatinisation commonly cited around 67 to 77 °C. Traditional brewers solve this by cooking part of the grain into a porridge first, then cooling it and adding fresh malt so the enzymes can work. It is the same logic as the cereal cooker in an Indian lager brewery handling rice and maize adjuncts.

Women have traditionally been the brewers in many of these communities. The skill is passed down through families. Recipes are adjusted by feel rather than by thermometer: how thick the porridge looks, how sour the mash smells, how lively the pot sounds. It is precise work, just measured with different instruments.

Many sorghum beers are soured on purpose. Brewers let lactic acid bacteria work on the cooked mash for a day or more before fermentation. That souring gives a refreshing tartness. It also lowers the pH, which helps keep harmful microbes out of a beer brewed without boiling equipment or refrigeration.

The finished beer is opaque because it is not filtered. It carries suspended starch, grain particles and live yeast. It is usually low in alcohol, often only a few percent. It also keeps fermenting in the pot. That is why it is drunk fresh. After a few days it turns too sour to enjoy.
From the pot to the carton

In southern Africa, opaque sorghum beer has been made commercially for decades. Because it is still fermenting when packed, it is sold in cartons with vented tops that let carbon dioxide escape. Drinkers shake the carton before drinking to mix the settled solids back in.

Elsewhere, brewers have used sorghum to make clear, lager-style beers, partly to rely on local grain rather than imported barley. Sorghum is also naturally gluten free, which is why it appears in many gluten-free beers worldwide.

Expect something closer to a tart, grainy porridge drink than a lager. Aroma is sour and bready, sometimes with notes of yoghurt or green apple. The body is thick, almost creamy, with grit from the grain. Carbonation is light and lively. Alcohol is gentle.

Freshness changes everything. On day one the beer is sweeter and softer. By day three it is sharper and stronger. Judging it the way you would judge a pilsner misses the point. The right question is whether it tastes clean, lively and fresh for its age.

Faults still exist. A smell of vinegar means acetic bacteria have taken hold, usually because the pot sat open too long. A rotten or cheesy note means the souring went wrong. A good brewer in a village knows these signs as well as any laboratory analyst does.

Sorghum beers show how much brewing comes down to the same few steps: convert starch, control acidity and ferment with whatever yeast is around. India has its own versions of that story, explored in our guides to traditional Indian rice beers and chicha and other corn beers.

For a first step, taste a sour wheat beer next to a plain wheat beer and focus on how acidity changes body and refreshment. That is the sensation at the heart of every traditional sorghum beer. Learning to describe it precisely is where structured sensory training starts.
